# Draft:Mox (Software)

----
}}
Mox is an open-source email server written in the Go programming language. It is designed as a monolithic, "all-in-one" application that consolidates the functionality of a Mail transfer agent (MTA), Mail delivery agent (MDA), spam filter, and webmail client into a single binary.
Mox diverges from the traditional "Unix philosophy" of email architecture, which typically relies on chaining distinct, loosely coupled software components (such as Postfix for transfer, Dovecot for delivery, and Rspamd for filtering). Instead, Mox aims to simplify deployment and maintenance for self-hosted environments and small-to-medium enterprises (SMEs) by internalizing these services.
Architecture
Mox is written in Go, leveraging the language's memory safety features to mitigate buffer overflow vulnerabilities common in legacy C-based MTAs. The software utilizes Go's goroutines to manage concurrency, allowing it to handle thousands of simultaneous connections with low memory overhead.
The server is distributed as a static binary with no external dependencies, allowing it to run across various distributions without conflict with system libraries.
Linux: Considered the primary deployment target. Mox includes utilities to generate systemd unit files for automated service management and integrates with standard Unix filesystem hierarchies.
macOS: Supported primarily for development and local testing. It is available via the MacPorts package manager.
Windows: While the binary can be compiled for Windows, the software lacks native integration with the Windows Service Control Manager, making it less suitable for production environments compared to Linux.
Features
Protocols
Mox implements modern standards while explicitly deprecating older protocols deemed obsolete or insecure.
SMTP: Implements a fully compliant MTA (RFC 5321). It supports standard submission ports (587) and implicit TLS (465), adhering to RFC 8314 recommendations.
IMAP: Supports IMAP4rev2 (RFC 9051) and extensions such as IDLE (RFC 2177) for real-time push notifications to clients.
POP3: Mox does not support POP3. The developers cite the protocol's inability to synchronize state (such as read status and sent folders) across multiple devices as the primary reason for its exclusion.
JMAP: Support for the JSON Meta Application Protocol is planned on the development roadmap.
Security
The server enforces a "secure by default" configuration.
Encryption: Defaults to TLS 1.3 and includes an integrated ACME client to automatically obtain and renew certificates from authorities like Let's Encrypt.
DANE: Mox includes first-class support for DNS-based Authentication of Named Entities (DANE). It validates TLSA records via DNSSEC on outbound mail to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks and publishes TLSA records for its own domains.
MTA-STS: Automatically serves MTA-STS policies and supports TLS Reporting (TLSRPT) to detect delivery failures caused by cryptographic issues.
Authentication: Uses an internal user database rather than system users (e.g., /etc/passwd) or external directories like LDAP. It supports SASL mechanisms including SCRAM-SHA-256 and PLAIN (over TLS).
Spam Filtering
Mox utilizes a "reputation-first" approach to spam filtering. It integrates an immediate feedback loop where moving messages to a "Junk" folder in an IMAP client instantly retrains the internal Bayesian filter.
Sender Identity: Automates the handling of SPF, DKIM, and DMARC. It generates necessary DNS records for administrators and enforces policies on incoming mail.
Tarpitting: The server employs "tarpitting" and traffic shaping to delay responses to suspicious IP addresses or repeated authentication failures, discouraging brute-force attacks.
